ABSTRACT Background The kynurenine pathway (KP) plays a pivotal role in many diseases that involve distinct pathological mechanisms. Objectives Since KP metabolites are potential disease biomarkers, it is crucial to investigate their fluctuations under physiological conditions. As the KP is stress‐responsive, this study examines how peripheral KP metabolites change with core temperature increases induced by two different modalities. Methods In this randomized cross‐over study, 11 young healthy males were subjected to (a) exogenous heating via hot water immersion (44°C, EXO), and (b) exertional heating via exercise (EXE), until rectal temperature ( T rec ) reached 39°C, followed by a recovery phase. Blood samples were collected at baseline and at every 0.5°C T rec increment during both the heating and recovery phases. Plasma levels of KP metabolites, stress, and metabolic markers were measured. Correlation analyses between kynurenine pathway metabolites and stress markers were computed over the course of the trials. Results EXE and EXO trials induced the KP, but to different extents. Most plasma KP metabolite concentrations (kynurenic acid, picolinic acid, 3‐hydrokynurenine, quinolinic acid) increased. Stress markers were elevated in both trials. Changes in KP metabolites, stress, and metabolic markers were not persistent, and returned to baseline following recovery. Funding: This work was supported by grants from the Vetenskapsrådet (2024‐02812), the Hjärnfonden (FO2022‐0140), Åhlén‐stiftelsen and the Initiative for Excellence in Universities Science and Sport Lithuania (No. S‐A‐UEI‐23‐2). 1 Introduction The kynurenine pathway (KP) is the primary route of tryptophan (TRP) degradation, generating physiologically active metabolites with diverse functions. While KP in the brain primarily originates from astrocytes, its peripheral activity is mainly localized in the liver and skeletal muscles. Metabolites produced along this pathway are increasingly recognized for their roles in neurological and psychiatric disorders, as well as playing a role in immune responses, cardiovascular function, and energy metabolism [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ]. Metabolites such as kynurenine (KYN), kynurenic acid (KYNA), quinolinic acid (QUIN), and picolinic acid (PIC) have been proposed as biomarkers for tracking disease severity and progression across various conditions [ 5 , 6 ]. Understanding the regulation of this pathway in healthy individuals, both at rest and under physiological stress, is essential for assessing its dysfunction in disease states. Physiological stressors such as exercise and caloric restriction have been shown to induce the KP, with cortisol identified as a trigger in this regard [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ]. Heat exposure, a universal physiological stressor, triggers thermoregulatory mechanisms and activates both neuronal and physiological processes [ 11 ]. Heat stress can be induced through exertional (EXE) means, such as exercise, which raises body temperature through muscle contraction and increased metabolic rates [ 12 ], or through exogenous (EXO) methods like hot‐water immersion [ 13 ]. Hot‐water immersion, a passive technique, is frequently used in both research and clinical settings to raise core body temperature without mechanical strain [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. Even slight increases in core temperature are thought to provoke a modest, but rapid, inflammatory response [ 15 , 16 ]. In addition to passive heating, exercise also produces stress‐induced immune activation, but with a more pronounced response [ 17 , 18 ]. In parallel, ample evidence indicates the activation of the kynurenine pathway by exercise or infection [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ]. From a functional perspective, if an increase in body temperature alone is a sufficient component to activate the KP, this could offer therapeutic potential for managing diseases involving dysregulation of the KP. It is well‐established that heat stress involves activation of both the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) and the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis. The SNS provides rapid adaptation to stressors through the release of catecholamines such as noradrenaline and adrenaline [ 24 ]. This response increases heart rate and redistributes blood flow to promote sweating and the regulation of body temperature. In contrast, the HPA axis triggers slower mechanisms involving cortisol production [ 25 ]. These responses are critical as both catecholamines and cortisol profoundly influence metabolism and immune functions, thereby impacting KP, especially under physiological stress [ 7 , 9 , 10 , 26 ]. While the majority of research on KP has been focused on its role in pathophysiological states [ 2 , 3 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ], relatively few studies have examined its regulation in healthy individuals, and among these, the majority have examined how exercise influences KP metabolites [ 9 , 10 , 31 , 32 ]. This study is the first to examine the effects of core temperature elevation on KP metabolites in healthy males. More specifically, the aim is to investigate the effects of two distinct heat stress modalities on KP metabolites. Additionally, we aim to examine whether well‐established stress markers would indirectly reflect the KP kinetics observed during the different heat stress modalities. To capture any delayed effects that might emerge post‐heating, samples were also collected during the recovery phase. We hypothesize that both passive heating and a rise in body temperature due to exercise will initiate a stress response, affecting the concentration of KP metabolites. We expect the EXE trial to produce more pronounced effects due to the additional cardiovascular, mechanical, and metabolic demands associated with exercise. Specifically, EXE uniquely activates skeletal muscle, a major source of peripheral KYNA, which should lead to higher plasma KYNA levels [ 8 , 32 ] than EXO. Additionally, we hypothesize that other biomarkers, such as catecholamines, will be particularly affected in the EXE trial and may parallel changes in KP metabolites, while prolactin levels are expected to be more responsive in the EXO trial due to its sensitivity to skin temperature [ 33 ].

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the impact of two distinct heat stress modalities—exertional heating (exercise/cycling) and exogenous heating (hot water immersion)—on physiological responses, stress markers, and peripheral kynurenine pathway (KP) metabolites in 11 young healthy males. Both modalities were designed to induce a comparable increase in core body temperature up to 39°C. The study found that heat exposure transiently induced the KP, elevating several plasma KP metabolite concentrations (Kynurenic acid, Picolinic acid, 3-Hydroxykynurenine, Quinolinic acid, Kynurenine, KYN/TRP ratio) and stress markers (Cortisol, Prolactin, Adrenaline, Noradrenaline, Lactate). These changes generally returned to baseline during recovery, suggesting adaptability of KP enzymes to physiological stressors. Differential changes were observed depending on the specific heat stress protocol and the phase (heating vs. recovery), with exertional heating often showing more pronounced effects for some markers and sustained elevation for others (e.g., KYNA, PIC in EXE). The study highlights the potential of KP metabolites as disease biomarkers.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Induced Hyperthermia / Heat Stress (Exertional heating and Exogenous heating)
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants underwent two distinct heat stress modalities: exertional heating (EXE) via cycling exercise at an intensity eliciting 60% VO2max in a 30°C room, and exogenous heating (EXO) via hot water immersion up to the waistline in a 44°C bath. Both trials were conducted until rectal temperature (Trec) reached 39°C (with measurements taken at every 0.5°C increment up to a maximum of 39.5°C), followed by a recovery phase to a baseline temperature of 37.5°C. The time required to reach specific temperature set points was similar in both trials. No direct dose-response comparisons were explicitly reported; however, EXE induced greater increases in stress markers and sympathetic vasomotor activity compared to EXO, suggesting differential physiological loads.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased in both EXE and EXO trials, peaking during the recovery phase at 38.5°C (EXE: p < 0.0001, from 52.9 nM to 83.7 nM; EXO: p < 0.05, from 52.6 nM to 65.7 nM). Concentrations steadily increased during the heating phase of the EXE trial and reached their peak during recovery. Unlike most other metabolites, KYNA did not revert to baseline levels upon returning to homeostatic temperatures. Detected in concentrations higher than the LLOQ of 5 nM.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Neuroprotective metabolite of the kynurenine pathway, involved in tryptophan degradation, neurological and psychiatric disorders, immune responses, cardiovascular function, and energy metabolism. It acts as an antagonist at glutamate receptors and modulates neurotransmission. Skeletal muscle is a major source of peripheral KYNA, with exercise stimulating PGC-1α expression and KAT enzyme activity, leading to increased peripheral KYNA levels.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Core temperature increases induced by exogenous heating (hot water immersion, 44°C) or exertional heating (exercise/cycling at 60% VO2max in a 30°C room), until rectal temperature reached 39°C, followed by a recovery phase. Samples collected at 0.5°C rectal temperature increments.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential disease biomarker whose fluctuations are important for assessing dysfunction. It indicates a potential neuroprotective response or modulation of neuronal excitability during recovery from heat stress. Higher plasma KYNA levels are hypothesized in EXE due to unique skeletal muscle activation. Its sustained elevation post-recovery may be due to relatively slow elimination via urine and is implicated in various diseases.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Only affected in the EXE trial, showing significant increases during heating and peaking at 38°C during recovery (p < 0.001). Concentrations steadily increased, with post-intervention levels remaining significantly different from baseline (p < 0.001) and from EXO trial levels (p < 0.05). Did not revert to baseline levels upon returning to homeostatic temperatures. Detected in concentrations higher than the LLOQ of 5 nM.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Metabolite of the kynurenine pathway, involved in tryptophan degradation, iron chelation, and modulation of immune function. PGC-1α induces ACMSD, the enzyme responsible for PIC production; elevated levels suggest increased acetyl-CoA synthesis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Core temperature increases induced by exertional heating (exercise/cycling at 60% VO2max in a 30°C room), until rectal temperature reached 39°C, followed by a recovery phase. Samples collected at 0.5°C rectal temperature increments.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential disease biomarker. Reflects kynurenine pathway activity and suggests elevated acetyl-CoA synthesis for energy generation. Its sustained elevation post-recovery may be due to relatively slow elimination via urine, indicating altered pathway flux and potential impact on mineral homeostasis and immune response under thermal stress.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Only affected in the EXE trial, showing a steady increase during the heating phase, which became more pronounced during recovery, peaking at 38°C (p < 0.001). Concentrations were detected higher than the LLOQ of 5 nM.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Metabolite of the kynurenine pathway, involved in tryptophan degradation, neurological and psychiatric disorders, immune responses, cardiovascular function, and energy metabolism. Known for its pro-oxidant and excitotoxic properties.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Core temperature increases induced by exertional heating (exercise/cycling at 60% VO2max in a 30°C room), until rectal temperature reached 39°C, followed by a recovery phase. Samples collected at 0.5°C rectal temperature increments.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential disease biomarker. Indicates activation of the kynurenine pathway towards potentially neurotoxic end-products, particularly under EXE stress. The transient increase and return to baseline suggest adaptability of KP enzymes to physiological stressors.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased during both EXE and EXO trials, peaking at 39°C (EXE) and 38.5°C during the recovery phase (EXO) (p < 0.05). Concentrations steadily increased during the heating phase of the EXE trial and reached their peak during the recovery phase. Reverted to baseline levels upon returning to homeostatic temperatures. Concentrations were detected higher than the LLOQ of 50 nM.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Neurotoxic metabolite of the kynurenine pathway, involved in tryptophan degradation, neurological and psychiatric disorders, immune responses, cardiovascular function, and energy metabolism. Acts as an N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor agonist, contributing to excitotoxicity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Core temperature increases induced by exogenous heating (hot water immersion, 44°C) or exertional heating (exercise/cycling at 60% VO2max in a 30°C room), until rectal temperature reached 39°C, followed by a recovery phase. Samples collected at 0.5°C rectal temperature increments.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Potential disease biomarker. Indicates the induction and activity of the kynurenine pathway due to physiological stress, as well as potential neuroinflammatory processes and neurotoxic risk under thermal stress. The transient increase and return to baseline suggest adaptability of KP enzymes to physiological stressors. Implicated in neurological, psychiatric, cardiovascular disorders, and cancer.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased upon both EXE and EXO, peaking at 39°C (p < 0.01) and returning to baseline. The greatest increase was observed during the EXO trial.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Stress hormone involved in various physiological processes, including immune modulation and osmoregulation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Heat stress (EXE and EXO trials) induced by core temperature increases, with samples collected at 0.5°C rectal temperature increments up to 39°C and subsequent decrease until 37.5°C.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates a physiological stress response to thermal load. Expected to be more responsive in EXO due to sensitivity to skin temperature.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Displayed a more pronounced and rapid elevation during the heating phase, peaking at 39°C (EXE: p < 0.01; EXO: p < 0.05) and returning to baseline at 37.5°C. The increase was greater in the EXE trial compared to the EXO trial (statistically significant in EXO, p < 0.05, but overall more pronounced in EXE).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Key catecholamine in the 'fight or flight' response, influencing cardiovascular function and metabolism, and triggering immediate stress responses via the Sympathetic Nervous System (SNS).
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Heat stress (EXE and EXO trials) induced by core temperature increases, with samples collected at 0.5°C rectal temperature increments up to 39°C and subsequent decrease until 37.5°C, particularly during the heating phases.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates acute sympathetic nervous system activation and stress response to thermal load. Higher levels in EXE likely indicate greater sympathetic vasomotor activity due to muscle strain from cycling.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Displayed a more pronounced and rapid elevation during the heating phase, peaking at 39°C in the EXE trial (p < 0.001) and returning to baseline at 37.5°C. In the EXO trial, the increase was smaller and not statistically significant (p > 0.05), although an overall increase in EXE was greater than EXO.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Catecholamine acting as a neurotransmitter and hormone, central to the sympathetic nervous system and stress response, triggering immediate stress responses via the SNS.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Heat stress (EXE and EXO trials) induced by core temperature increases, with samples collected at 0.5°C rectal temperature increments up to 39°C and subsequent decrease until 37.5°C, particularly during the heating phases.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Essential amino acid, precursor for serotonin and kynurenine pathway metabolites, influencing mood and immunity.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Heat stress (EXE and EXO trials) induced by core temperature increases, with samples collected at 0.5°C rectal temperature increments up to 39°C and subsequent decrease until 37.5°C, particularly during heating and recovery phases.

Detected in concentrations higher than the LLOQ of 50 nM.

Post-intervention levels were significantly different between trials (p < 0.01). Detected in concentrations higher than the LLOQ of 50 nM.
